title: The Sheep and the Goats
hook: Is the parable of the sheep and goats really about believers escaping hellfire?
tldr: Matthew 25:31-46 is a parable judging nations by how they treat the poor, not individuals by their beliefs. Faith is never mentioned, so reading it as hell would make salvation depend on works. Echoing Ezekiel 34 and Zechariah 10:3, the goats are Israel's selfish leaders, and older translations render verse 46 as age-long correction, not endless torment.
big_idea: A shepherd disciplines his goats; he does not torture them with fire.

points.title: A parable, not a news report
points.text: Like the Ten Virgins and the Bags of Gold before it, this is a parable, not a historiographical account of future events.

points.title: Judged for neglecting the needy
points.text: The warning is not about flawed doctrine or lack of faith but indifference to the hungry, stranger, sick and imprisoned, and it was aimed at the religious community.

points.title: Nations, not individuals
points.text: All the nations are gathered. Nations cannot burn in hell, but they can collapse and be consumed in 'everlasting fire', like empires permanently destroyed.

points.title: A problem for sola fide
points.text: Faith is never mentioned. If this were about escaping hell, salvation would come through deeds like visiting prisons, contradicting the Reformed doctrine of faith alone.

points.title: Goats are selfish shepherds
points.text: Ezekiel 34 and Zechariah 10:3 use goats for Israel's self-serving leaders. Jesus, like the prophets, judges Israel's leadership for neglecting the poor.

points.title: Age-long correction
points.text: Older translations render verse 46 as onian chastisement, punishment age-during, long correction or age-abiding correction, not everlasting torment.

sections.summary: Matthew 25 holds three parables: the Ten Virgins (1-13), the Bags of Gold (14-28) and the Sheep and the Goats (31-46). Some, Augustine included, read verses 41-46 as proof of Augustinian-Calvinist hellfire. In the parable the Son of Man gathers all nations and separates sheep from goats. The sheep fed, welcomed, clothed and visited 'the least of these'; the goats did not, and go to aionion (age-long) fire and punishment.

sections.h: First and second: a parable aimed at the religious
sections.summary: First, this, like the two before it, is a parable, not a historical account. Second, Jesus' warning is not aimed at people with flawed soteriology or Christology, nor at those lacking faith in him, but at those indifferent to society's marginalized, impoverished and needy. The original audience and critique were the religious community, not secular, non-believing society.

Verse 32 says the nations are gathered. Nations cannot burn in hell, but they can collapse and be consumed by enemies in 'everlasting fire', like empires permanently destroyed. Historically, nations that neglected their poor and needy often foreshadowed their own destruction. Abbott's An Analytical Study of Words says the passage concerns the judgment of nations, not individuals, distinct from other judgments in Scripture.

The text has no redemptive quality and no hint of post-mortem salvation. If it were about salvation from hell, salvation would come not through faith, never mentioned, but through deeds like visiting prisons and clothing the homeless. That is a dilemma for Augustinian-Calvinist damnation: torment would hinge on actions, not faith, contradicting the Reformed doctrine of sola fide, 'by faith alone'.

In the Middle East sheep are cuter and tastier than goats, but that is not the key difference. The key is the Hebrew Scriptures. Ezekiel 34 prophesies woe to Israel's shepherds who only care for themselves, and God judges between sheep, rams and goats. It is not believers versus seculars but a critique of Israel's leaders and poor stewardship. Zechariah 10:3 (KJV) says God punished the goats; NIV and ESV oddly omit 'goats'.

Like the prophets, Jesus' judgment parables target Israel and its leaders, accountable for the poor, widows and orphans. Two chapters earlier, in Matthew 23, he denounces them with Ezekiel's language of woes. The chief priests and Pharisees knew his parables were about them. Reading them as unbelievers versus believers makes no sense, since Jesus had not yet died. The kingdom would be taken from them and given to a people producing fruit.

Jesus gave the keys of the Kingdom to his Jewish followers, moving God's presence from man-made sects to his own. The first church was mostly Israeli Jews, countering Replacement Theology: God created a new Jewish denomination into which Gentiles were integrated. A shepherd does not torture or kill annoying goats but disciplines them. Goats may be wicked leaders, bad nations or both, facing disciplinary punishment.

Kolasin aionion is treated elsewhere, but older translations of Matthew 25:46 speak plainly: Hanson 1884, onian chastisement; Young's 1898, punishment age-during; Modern English 1903, a long correction; People's New Covenant 1925, age-continuing correction; 1938, eonian correction; Rotherham 1959 and Sacred Name Bible 1976, age-abiding correction; 1980, a new period of suffering. With over 900 English translations, comparing versions broadens understanding.

notes.note: The goats: nations or leaders who neglected the hungry, stranger, sick and imprisoned, not unbelievers.
Aionion means age-long; older translations render it onian chastisement or age-abiding correction.
The same word describes life; the parable judges deeds, and faith is never mentioned.

quiz.q: Why are the goats condemned in the parable?
options: Neglecting the hungry, strangers, sick and imprisoned
quiz.why: Faith is never mentioned; the issue is indifference to the marginalized, a critique aimed at the religious community.

quiz.q: Which prophet's sheep-and-goats imagery targets Israel's selfish shepherds?
quiz.why: Ezekiel 34 pronounces woe on shepherds who only care for themselves and judges between rams and goats.

quiz.q: How did Young's Literal Translation (1898) render Matthew 25:46?
quiz.why: Young's has 'punishment age-during, but the righteous to life age-during', reflecting aionion as age-related.

reflect: If this parable judges how communities treat the poor, what would it say about your community today?
